pr.title: Add a test for trait solver overflow in MIR inliner cycle detection
pr.description:
This test is a combination of the reproducer posted here: https://github.com/rust-lang/rust/issues/128887#issuecomment-2314198229 and the existing test for polymorphic recursion: https://github.com/rust-lang/rust/blob/784d444733d65c3d305ce5edcbb41e3d0d0aee2e/tests/mir-opt/inline/polymorphic_recursion.rs

r? @compiler-errors
pr.author: saethlin

classification.name: Inline
evidence: the existing test for polymorphic recursion

The added regression test is specifically for the MIR inliner: it lives under tests/mir-opt/inline, enables the inliner with -Zinline-mir, and was derived from the existing polymorphic recursion inliner test. The concrete Inline MirPass implementation is present at this revision.

processing.reason: PR #129757 is test-only: it adds tests/mir-opt/inline/type_overflow.rs with `// skip-filecheck` and `-Zinline-mir`, asserting only that compilation completes without a trait-solver overflow during MIR inliner cycle detection. The historical failure mode is a compile-time query/overflow, and the diff contains no replaced MIR pass or value-level rewrite. There is therefore no source-grounded ORIGINAL-vs-INCORRECT pair of same-signature Rust functions whose concrete return values legitimately differ; constructing one (e.g., an unrelated recursion or overflow simulation) would manufacture a transformation not present in the PR.

analysis.summary: Regression-test-only PR for MIR inliner cycle detection: polymorphic recursive calls through an associated-type chain must not drive the trait solver into overflow when -Zinline-mir is enabled. The reusable knowledge is the focused compile-success test shape, not a MIR-output change.
analysis.originalLogic: The MIR inliner's cycle-detection strategy must decide whether to inline recursive calls such as recurse::<T::Chain>() without repeatedly asking the trait solver to normalize an ever-growing associated-type chain. The added test checks that the strategy in #129714 "avoids trait solver overflows in this specific case" while compiling with `-Zinline-mir`.
analysis.incorrectTransformation: The historically problematic inliner behavior was that cycle detection did not sufficiently guard recursive polymorphic inlining, so inlining/analyzing `recurse::<T::Chain>()` could cause the trait solver to overflow on the recursive associated-type chain. This is a compile-time query divergence/overflow during inlining, not a silently wrong MIR value rewrite; the patch itself only adds the regression test and does not show a replaced rewrite.
analysis.inputDomain: Generic Rust code compiled with the MIR inliner enabled (`-Zinline-mir`), containing a recursive generic function whose recursive call instantiates a type obtained from an associated type, under a trait whose associated-type bound recursively references the same associated type.
analysis.trigger: A generic function `recurse<T: Foo<Associated = f64>>()` calls an extension method on `T` and then calls `recurse::<T::Chain>()`, where `Foo::Chain: Foo<Associated = Self::Associated>`; multiple callers are emitted to increase the chance that cycle detection encounters the recursive polymorphic inlining case under `-Zinline-mir`.
preconditions: The MIR inliner is enabled with `-Zinline-mir`.
A trait has an associated type whose bound recursively constrains `Associated` through `Self::Associated`.
A generic function recursively calls itself with an associated-type projection (`T::Chain`).
Several caller functions are emitted so the bug is more likely to be observed.
pitfalls: Do not treat this as a MIR-output correctness case: the test uses `// skip-filecheck`, so it checks successful compilation/cycle handling rather than expected MIR text.
Do not infer that a retained test name or comment proves a replacement pass is wrong; this PR adds a new test only.
A single caller may not reliably exercise the overflow path, hence the macro-generated batch of entry points.
The failure mode is a trait-solver overflow during inliner cycle detection, not a local borrowing or overwrite issue in generated MIR.
Do not generalize this observation to unrelated optimization passes; the source is specifically about the Inline MIR pass.
analysis.testStrategy: Add a `tests/mir-opt/inline` regression test compiled with `-Zinline-mir` and `// skip-filecheck`. Define a trait `Foo` with `type Associated` and `type Chain: Foo<Associated = Self::Associated>`, an extension trait implemented for `T: Foo<Associated = f64>`, and a recursive `recurse<T: Foo<Associated = f64>>()` that calls `T::do_ext()` then `recurse::<T::Chain>()`. Use a macro to emit many public callers (`m00` through `m19`) to increase the chance of triggering the bug. The focused assertion is simply that the compiler completes without a trait solver overflow; no MIR FileCheck expectations are needed.
